name: plangate-required-routes-to-declared-permission
description:
A `required` type routes approval to the permission it DECLARES, not to a hardcoded relation name.

maintrepo_repo declares standing: required with approverPermission: maintainer, and NOTHING is seeded anywhere — no bootstrap, no tuple on maintainer_ref, none on owner. The approval therefore fails closed, and the assertion is on WHICH subject-set the refusal names: it must be "#maintainer". A router still building "<type>:<id>#owner", as four call sites did, names "#owner" and this bundle fails.

Proving the routing through a SUCCESSFUL approval would need a seeded tuple and a click, and would then pass for the wrong reason if anything downstream went permissive. The refusal names the set directly and cannot.

The hardcode was why two very different types looked identical to the router: crm_company's `owner` is a real computed permission backed by seeded tuples, while git_repo's `owner` is a bare relation declared only so the checks are answerable and never populated. The router could not tell governance from schema shape, and a push to a git remote became permanently unapprovable (observed live 2026-08-21). `maintainer` here is both differently named AND a computed permission, so it covers that distinction too.

The push tool is stateImpact:external so it re-approves per call and reaches the approval builder rather than being satisfied by a plan-gate grant. Asserted on the TOOL RESULT, never the reply — a scripted transcript says the same words whether the call pushed or refused.
